meta.subtitle: Pre-profit NDAA-compliant drone-component maker; Q2 revenue up 687% to $16.7M, priced near 35.6x sales with margins still deeply negative.

analystCommentary: Our rating on Unusual Machines is BUY, with a 12-month target range of $25.00 to $42.00 versus the current $22.69. The call rests on demand, not profitability: {+ Q2 2026 revenue reached $16,722,467, up 687% from $2,123,970 a year earlier +}, and consensus models FY26E revenue of about $56.4M (+404%). The company is not profitable. Q2 loss from operations was approximately $7.8 million and the trailing-twelve-month operating margin is -93.5%, so the -141.8x P/E and a blank EV/EBITDA carry no signal. What supports the equity is the balance sheet and the order pipeline: {+ cash was approximately $229.6 million at June 30, 2026, up from $103.3 million +} at December 31, 2025, and management targets positive cash flow from normal operations, as adjusted, by the end of 2026. The offsetting risk is valuation: at 35.6x sales the price already embeds years of flawless execution, and {- our Bear case of $13.00 sits well below the current price -}. We rate the shares a BUY but size them for a wide band of outcomes.

executiveSummary.companyOverview: Unusual Machines, Inc. (NYSE American: UMAC) manufactures and sells drone components and drones across a brand portfolio that includes Fat Shark FPV video goggles and the Rotor Riot ecommerce store. It sells through B2B, e-commerce, and retail channels and positions itself as a domestic, NDAA-compliant Tier-1 parts supplier to the U.S. drone industry. The company was incorporated in 2019, was formerly known as AerocarveUS Corporation, took its current name in July 2022, and is headquartered in Orlando, Florida. It reports as a single segment; FY25 revenue was $11.2M, up 101.2%. The business is scaling quickly from a small base: headcount grew from 81 to 141 employees in the first quarter of 2026, reached 240 at the end of the second quarter, and exceeds 255 today. Management has begun in-house manufacturing of drone motors, headsets, cameras and other components, and signed a definitive agreement on May 7, 2026 to acquire DroneNX, LLC (operating as Upgrade Energy), a maker of battery and power systems, for an estimated $52.0 million. The company also has a strategic collaboration with Lantronix Inc. on autonomous drone components integrating edge AI compute with flight control systems.

thesis.body: The thesis is a bet on domestic drone-component demand outrunning a rich valuation. Revenue is compounding from a small base, at $16,722,467 in Q2 2026 versus $2,123,970 a year earlier, and the growth is now led by enterprise sales rather than the legacy retail channel. The demand signals are external as well as internal: the Drone Dominance program is a $1.1 billion Department of War program in which management says over half of the participants are Unusual Machines customers. Against this, the stock trades at 35.6x sales while the Q2'26 operating margin is -47%, and the share count is rising through an at-the-market program and acquisition stock. Our BUY reflects the demand evidence and the $229.6 million cash cushion; the wide target range and a real Bear case reflect how much execution the price already assumes.

catalysts: Closing the Upgrade Energy acquisition, targeted by the end of the third quarter, would add domestic battery and power-system manufacturing; the deal is estimated at $52.0 million and is contingent on Upgrade Energy completing its audit, expected in September 2026.

The fourth-quarter manufacturing ramp: management plans to increase motor production capacity in Q4, says the equipment is already in the country, and expects major Drone Dominance demand to begin hitting in September.
A gross-margin recovery toward the stated 40% target, which management expects after production margins dip from the 34.7% reported in Q2 during a Q3 investment quarter.
Reaching positive cash flow from normal operations, as adjusted, which management targets by the end of 2026.
risks: Valuation: the shares trade on sales rather than earnings, so any slowdown in growth can compress the multiple sharply.
Dilution: the share count is climbing through the at-the-market program, the Upgrade Energy stock consideration, and the July 2026 equity grants, which steadily dilutes existing holders.
Customer concentration: one customer was approximately 42% of Q2 2026 revenue, so the loss of that account would be material.
Supplier dependence: the company relies on a limited number of suppliers with no long-term binding contracts, a risk flagged in the 10-K.
A deliberate Q3 pause: management says it does not expect Q3 revenue to follow the historical quarterly pattern as it does foundational scaling work.

financials.incomeCommentary: The income statement is a growth-at-a-loss profile. Q2 2026 revenue was $16,722,467, {+ up 687% +} from $2,123,970 a year earlier, an increase of $14,598,497; for the six months, revenue was $24,818,304 versus $4,166,270, up 496%. Enterprise sales drove the quarter, at $14,220,865 versus $192,090 a year earlier. Gross profit rose to $5,802,134 from $794,679, but {- gross margin slipped to 34.7% from 37.4% -} as the company onshored manufacturing. Operating expense remains the problem: Q2 general and administrative expense alone was $10,799,261, up 50% from $7,195,193, research and development was $430,759 (up 587%), and sales and marketing was $790,012 (up 161%). The result was a Q2 net loss of $7,783,553, {- slightly wider than the $6,964,739 loss a year earlier -}. Management notes the GAAP operating loss of approximately $7.8 million was dominated by non-cash stock compensation of approximately $5.7 million, and reports an adjusted EBITDA loss of only about $0.4 million. On a trailing-twelve-month basis the gross margin is 34.8%, the operating margin is -93.5%, and the net margin is -20.3%. FY25 diluted EPS was $-0.74, and consensus expects losses to continue, with FY26E EPS of $-0.21 and FY27E EPS of $-0.32.
financials.balanceCommentary: The balance sheet is the strongest part of the story. {+ Cash was approximately $229.6 million at June 30, 2026, up from $103.3 million +} at December 31, 2025, lifted by equity raises rather than operations. Management cites working capital of approximately $367.5 million at quarter-end. The Facts pack shows no total debt or net debt for any year, and the trailing current ratio is 53.82, so near-term liquidity is not the concern; dilution is. Inventory is building ahead of the ramp: raw materials and prepaid inventory rose from $25.8 million at March 31, 2026 to $42.4 million at June 30, 2026, and finished inventory rose from $1.6 million to $4.4 million. That inventory build is the mechanism the company is using to convert cash into future sales, and it is also the working-capital risk if demand slips.
financials.cashflowCommentary: Cash flow tells the pre-profit story plainly. On a trailing basis the FCF yield is -5.2%, FY25 free cash flow was -$23.2M against capital expenditure of -$2.1M, and the FY25 FCF margin was -207.5%. The company spent approximately $3.3 million on capex in Q2 2026, chiefly to automate its motor line. Management frames the near-term picture around adjusted figures, noting the business was cash-flow positive in the first half of 2026 once interest income and realized gains from short-term investments are included, while still running an operating loss. Those investment items are volatile: the six months included a realized gain from short-term investments of $9.5 million and an unrealized gain of $5.6 million, and Q2 carried an unrealized loss on investments of approximately $3.9 million, so they are not a durable source of cash. The letter sets two separate milestones, and I use both as stated: positive cash flow from normal operations, as adjusted, targeted by the end of 2026, and the higher breakeven point, which the CEO believes the company can reach by the end of the first quarter of 2027. Interest income of approximately $1.8 million in Q2, versus $0.2 million a year earlier, shows the large cash balance is at least self-funding part of the burn.

valuation.multiplesCommentary: Traditional multiples are not usable here. The trailing P/E is -141.8x and the forward P/E is negative (-110.7x on an NTM basis) because the company loses money; EV/EBITDA is not meaningful. The one multiple that works is price-to-sales, at 35.6x, and it is demanding: the market capitalization of about $1.1B rests on FY25 revenue of $11.2M and consensus FY26E revenue of about $56.4M. In other words, the shares are valued on a revenue base the company has not yet earned. We therefore anchor valuation on revenue growth, the gross-margin path toward the stated 40% target, and the cash runway, not on earnings multiples. The peer set available in the data is not comparable to an operating drone-parts business, so we do not lean on relative multiples. Consensus target prices span $30.00 to $45.00 with a $39.00 mean, implying about 71.9% upside; we view that as achievable only in our Bull case and set a more conservative central range.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: Execution stays on the current trajectory: the Q4 motor ramp lands, Drone Dominance demand converts, revenue tracks toward the FY27E consensus of $112.2M, and gross margin recovers toward the 40% target. On those results the market keeps paying a premium multiple and the shares re-rate toward the top of the current consensus range.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: Growth continues but decelerates through the planned Q3 investment quarter, FY26E revenue lands near the $56.4M consensus, and losses narrow without yet turning positive. The price-to-sales multiple compresses from 35.6x as the early premium fades, leaving the stock modestly above today's $22.69.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: Demand converts more slowly than the pipeline implies, the Q3 pause extends, gross margin stays under its target, and continued equity issuance dilutes holders. A pre-profit name on such a rich sales multiple de-rates hard in that environment, and the shares fall back toward the lower half of the 52-week range of $7.25 to $34.93.

valuation.scenarioCommentary: Weighting the three cases at 30% Bull, 40% Base, and 30% Bear yields a probability-weighted fair value of about $28.60, roughly 26% above the current $22.69, with a reward-to-risk ratio below one because the Bear downside of about 43% is larger than the expected upside. That asymmetry is deliberate: for a pre-profit company trading at a rich multiple of sales, the distribution of outcomes is wide, and the Bear at $13.00 is a genuine scenario, not a formality. Our target range of $25.00 to $42.00 brackets the Base case and sits below the consensus mean, reflecting more caution on multiple compression than the Street carries. The call is a BUY because the demand evidence and a large cash balance tilt the expected value positive, but it is a call to hold with a wide band of outcomes in mind.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: Unusual Machines reports as a single segment, so the revenue mix is the consolidated total rather than a product or geographic split. FY25 revenue was $11.2M, all consolidated. Within that, the business spans in-house manufactured components, including drone motors, headsets and cameras, and its consumer brands, Fat Shark FPV goggles and the Rotor Riot store. The shift underway is from retail toward enterprise, and as the income discussion shows, the enterprise channel now dominates the quarter. Customer concentration is high while that shift is young; one customer was about 42% of Q2 revenue and the best-selling product about 13%.

moatFactors.name: Domestic, NDAA-compliant supply position
moatFactors.body: The company positions itself as a domestic, NDAA-compliant Tier-1 parts supplier, and its Q2 growth was driven by NDAA and Blue UAS products. Policy is reinforcing this: the shareholder letter cites an FCC ban on light-show and swarming drones and a $1.1 billion Department of War Drone Dominance program in which management says over half of the participants are its customers. Domestic-sourcing rules are hard for foreign-dependent competitors to satisfy quickly, which is a real if early advantage.

moatFactors.name: Consumer brands (Fat Shark, Rotor Riot)
moatFactors.body: In FPV, the company owns Fat Shark, described as a leader in ultra-low-latency FPV video goggles, and the Rotor Riot ecommerce store. These give it a recognized retail foothold and direct customer relationships, though retail is now the smaller and slower-growing side of the business as the mix shifts to enterprise.

moatFactors.name: Manufacturing scale and vertical integration
moatFactors.body: The company is building in-house manufacturing of motors, headsets and cameras and adding battery capacity via the pending Upgrade Energy acquisition. Scale advantages are not yet proven, with Q2 gross margin at 34.7%, below the 40% target, but vertical integration could become a cost advantage if volumes rise as management expects.

businessMoat.durability: The durability of any advantage here is unproven. The company's own risk factors say it faces competition from larger companies with substantially greater resources and that it operates in an emerging, rapidly evolving industry that is difficult to evaluate. Its strongest edge, domestic and NDAA-compliant sourcing at a moment when U.S. policy favors it, depends on regulation and defense procurement that could change. It also relies on a limited number of suppliers without long-term binding contracts, which caps how defensible the supply chain really is today. The most credible path to durability is converting the current demand surge into installed manufacturing scale and repeat enterprise relationships before better-funded rivals do; the $229.6 million cash balance buys time to try. Until margins and free cash flow turn positive, we treat the moat as narrow and contingent rather than established.

points: Revenue is compounding fast off a small base: Q2 2026 revenue of $16,722,467 was {+ up 687% year over year +} and 106% over Q1 2026, and the six-month total was $24,818,304, up 496%.
Enterprise is the engine: for the six months, enterprise revenue was $21,510,234 versus $312,246 a year earlier, and it now outweighs the retail channel it is displacing.
Consensus expects the ramp to continue, modeling FY26E revenue of about $56.4M (+404%) and FY27E revenue of $112.2M.

Capacity is being added deliberately: headcount rose from 81 to 141 in Q1 2026, to 240 at the end of Q2, and to more than 255 today, and management plans to expand motor production in Q4 with equipment already in the country.

External demand vehicles are large: beyond the $1.1 billion Drone Dominance program, the shareholder letter cites a $500 million follow-on contract for Neros under the PBAS program and an $820 million Office of Strategic Capital loan vehicle for PDW as signs of sector demand.
The addressable market is large: the letter cites Fact.MR sizing the global drone accessories market at $25.2 billion today, reaching $156 billion by 2034.

management.leadership: Unusual Machines is led by CEO Allan Evans, who signs the quarterly shareholder letter and sits on the board. The proxy identifies the other named executive officers as Brian Hoff, Andrew Camden and Jeffrey Thompson; Thompson previously served as CEO and remains a director. Management's communication is detailed and candid about the trade-offs of scaling: it warns that Q3 2026 revenue will not follow the historical quarterly pattern because labor and capacity are being redirected to foundational work, and it states plainly that production margins will decline from the 34.7% reported in Q2 before recovering in Q4. That willingness to guide down a quarter to invest is a positive signal on operating discipline, though the story still depends on execution the company has not yet delivered at the promised scale.
management.capitalAllocation: Capital allocation is dominated by equity issuance and reinvestment, not returns to shareholders; the dividend yield is 0.00%. In May 2026 the company sold 2,000,000 shares at $30.00 through an at-the-market facility for $60.0 million of gross proceeds, about $58.2 million net, part of what management calls a staircase financing strategy. It is deploying that capital into the inventory build noted in the balance-sheet discussion, into the capital equipment behind its motor line covered in the cash-flow discussion, and into the pending $52.0 million Upgrade Energy acquisition, which is structured largely in stock (1,792,012 shares at $13.9508) plus cash tied to a $10.0 million battery-revenue milestone. The approach funds growth but steadily dilutes existing holders, which is the central cost of the strategy.
management.governance: Governance rests on the DEF 14A filed 2025-10-20. The board has three standing committees, Audit, Compensation, and Corporate Governance and Nominating, and held 13 meetings during 2024. The board determined that all present directors are independent except Dr. Evans, who is not independent because he is CEO, and Mr. Thompson, who is not independent having been CEO within the prior three years. The Audit Committee comprises Mr. Rich (Chair), Mr. Lowry and Ms. Colon, all independent. Related-party dealings are disclosed: in November 2024 the company took a purchase order from Teal Drones, a subsidiary of Red Cat whose CEO, Jeff Thompson, sits on the Unusual Machines board, recognizing $155,000 of revenue in 2024 and $55,000 in the first half of 2025 on a $250,000 contract. In May 2025, Evans and three directors invested an aggregate $420,000 in a company offering. These items are small but worth monitoring given the overlapping roles.
management.insiderOwnership: Insider ownership is modest. As of the October 6, 2025 record date, when 33,101,445 shares were outstanding, all executive officers and directors as a group (7 persons) held 2,466,617 shares, or 7.5%. CEO Allan Evans held 1,130,228 shares (3.4%). The July 24, 2026 equity grants, including 5,000,000 performance warrants to the CEO exercisable at $25 and vesting only as the stock reaches $25 through $100, plus stock options to other executives and employees at $19.36, are designed to tie insiders to share-price appreciation, though the CEO warrant grant is subject to shareholder approval and would add to dilution if the price targets are hit.

idiosyncratic: Valuation and dilution together: the stock trades at 35.6x sales and a -141.8x trailing P/E while the share count keeps rising through the at-the-market program, the $52.0 million Upgrade Energy stock consideration, and the July 2026 option and warrant grants. If growth slows, both the multiple and per-share value can fall at once.
Customer and product concentration: a single customer was about 42% of Q2 2026 revenue and the best-selling product about 13%, so the loss of one account or program would be felt immediately.

Execution and margin risk: the company is standing up new motor, camera and battery lines at once, management expects gross margin to fall from 34.7% before recovering, and the 40% target may not be reached until late 2026 or early 2027; any slippage pushes the milestones out.

Supply-chain fragility: the 10-K flags reliance on a limited number of suppliers without long-term binding contracts, so a shortage could delay product delivery during the very ramp the thesis depends on.

Deal and audit risk: the Upgrade Energy acquisition is contingent on the target completing an audit expected in September 2026 and on customary closing conditions, so the added battery capacity is not yet certain.
risks.systemic: Systemic risks center on policy and the cycle. The bull case leans heavily on U.S. defense and regulatory tailwinds, including the Drone Dominance program, the FCC ban on light-show and swarming drones, and domestic-sourcing preferences, all of which are set by government and could shift with budgets or administrations. The 10-K also warns that rising tariffs or trade-policy uncertainty could disrupt the supply chain and that FAA or other regulatory approvals could constrain how drones are used. As a small, pre-profit, recently volatile stock, with a 52-week range running from $7.25 to $34.93, UMAC is also exposed to swings in risk appetite for speculative growth names; a broad de-rating of unprofitable companies would hit the multiple regardless of company execution.

body: We rate Unusual Machines a BUY, with a target range of $25.00 to $42.00 set below the Street's consensus mean. The recommendation follows the expected value of our three scenarios: their probability-weighted fair value sits well above today's price, even as the company remains deeply unprofitable. The evidence for the call is demand and liquidity, namely the quarter's revenue surge, the enterprise-led mix, and a large cash balance with no debt, as detailed in the sections above.

This is a position to size for volatility, not a high-conviction anchor. The reward-to-risk profile is deliberately skewed toward a larger drawdown than upside, as set out in the scenario discussion, which is the right shape for a pre-profit business trading on sales rather than earnings. The main things to watch are the Q4 manufacturing ramp, the gross-margin recovery management has guided, the closing of the Upgrade Energy acquisition, and the two cash-flow milestones the letter sets, positive cash flow from normal operations by the end of 2026 and the breakeven point by the end of the first quarter of 2027. If those land, the Bull case opens up; if they slip, the Bear is real.
